nameStory: Squirrel corn gets its charming name from the small, yellow underground bulblets that look remarkably like tiny kernels of corn. These little "corns" are actually storage organs that help the plant survive through winter, and they're said to be a favorite food of squirrels and chipmunks who dig them up in early spring.
description: Squirrel corn is a delicate spring wildflower that emerges from the forest floor like a fairy garden in miniature. This low-growing plant reaches only 6-12 inches tall, with lacy, blue-green leaves that look almost fern-like in their fine divisions. The oddly shaped white flowers dangle like tiny hearts or pantaloons from arching stems, creating an enchanting display that lasts just a few weeks in early spring.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White heart-shaped flowers with two rounded spurs at the base, hanging like tiny pantaloons from arching stems. Each flower is about half an inch long and feels papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Finely divided, lacy blue-green leaves that feel soft and delicate, almost like feathers. The leaves emerge from the ground on their own stems, separate from the flower stalks.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant that rarely exceeds 12 inches tall, forming small colonies connected by underground bulblets. Dies back completely by midsummer, leaving no trace above ground.

idTips.label: Underground Parts
idTips.description: Small yellow bulblets that look exactly like tiny corn kernels, clustered together underground. These feel firm and smooth when carefully excavated.

habitat: Look for squirrel corn in rich, moist deciduous forests with deep leaf litter, especially on north-facing slopes and in ravines. It thrives in the same areas as trilliums and wild ginger, preferring neutral to slightly alkaline soil. You'll often find it growing alongside its cousin, Dutchman's breeches, in the same woodland communities.

seasonality.spring: Blooms from April to May, with flowers appearing just as the leaves emerge. This is the only time of year you can see the plant above ground, making it a true spring ephemeral.
seasonality.summer: Completely disappears by midsummer, going dormant until the following spring. Only the underground bulblets remain active, storing energy for next year's growth.
seasonality.fall: No above-ground presence. The bulblets are developing underground, preparing for the next spring's emergence.
seasonality.winter: Dormant season with only the corn-like bulblets surviving underground, protected by the forest's leaf litter and snow cover.

funFact: Squirrel corn is essentially a botanical time traveler - it completes its entire above-ground life cycle in just 6-8 weeks, then vanishes completely for 10 months of the year, surviving solely on energy stored in its tiny corn-kernel bulblets buried in the soil.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Dutchman's breeches, which often grows in the same locations and has similar lacy leaves. The key difference is in the flowers: squirrel corn has heart-shaped flowers with rounded spurs, while Dutchman's breeches look exactly like tiny white pantaloons hanging upside down with pointed spurs. Memory trick: squirrel corn flowers are more heart-shaped like a corn kernel, while Dutchman's breeches really do look like pants.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "corn," this plant is completely unrelated to the corn we eat and belongs to the poppy family. The bulblets were historically eaten by Native Americans after proper preparation, but modern foragers should avoid them as they can be toxic if not prepared correctly.
compareHints: Squirrel corn differs from Dutchman's breeches primarily in flower shape - squirrel corn has heart-shaped flowers with rounded spurs, while Dutchman's breeches has pantaloon-shaped flowers with pointed spurs. The underground storage organs also differ: squirrel corn has clustered yellow bulblets that look like corn kernels, while Dutchman's breeches has white, teardrop-shaped bulbs. Both species have similarly divided, lacy leaves and the same ephemeral spring lifestyle.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to squirrel corn, Dutchman's breeches has more distinctly "pantaloon-shaped" flowers with pointed spurs versus squirrel corn's heart-shaped blooms with rounded spurs.

Fringed bleeding heart differs from its cousins Dutchman's breeches and squirrel corn by blooming throughout the growing season rather than just early spring, and by its pink heart-shaped flowers instead of white pantaloon or kernel-shaped blooms.
Pacific Bleeding Heart differs from its New England relatives by blooming later and longer than the early spring ephemerals Dutchman's Breeches and Squirrel Corn, which go dormant by early summer.
